items.question: How do you understand the role of compositionality in learning to handle new situations?
items.object: Compositionality in learning
items.answer: Compositionality has a lot of different meanings in different situations. The way that I think we're using it in the work that we're doing right now is that you have atomic knowledge that you maybe learned in one situation, but then you can build bigger structures out of those little pieces of knowledge in order to extrapolate to new situations that might even be out of distribution. I think that's really important for being able to learn in environments that are not totally new. It's not like you can plop yourself in a totally new world and immediately be fully competent. But if you're in a world that is changing, where the building blocks are the same and the causal mechanisms are being reused, then compositionality—and ways of having knowledge that can be broken into pieces and then recombined for new situations—is really crucial.

The response identifies changing environments that reuse underlying causal mechanisms as settings where compositional knowledge is especially important for adaptation.

items.question: How do you understand Elizabeth Spelke’s idea of a “curse of a compositional mind”?
items.object: Compositionality and Elizabeth Spelke’s “curse of a compositional mind”
items.answer: What she's pointing out is that compositionality is a kind of double-edged sword. We saw this in the first wave of symbolic AI, when people tried to build these compositional production systems to solve problems. The issue is you immediately encounter this combinatorial explosion in the number of things that you could represent, and you don't necessarily have any way of steering yourself through that space toward the kinds of concepts that are probable or which make sense in your current situation. So you can kind of think infinitely many things. Things might be very out of distribution. You're both immensely powerful but immensely overwhelmed by possibilities.
quotes: What she's pointing out is that compositionality is a kind of double-edged sword. We saw this in the first wave of symbolic AI, when people tried to build these compositional production systems to solve problems.

The issue is you immediately encounter this combinatorial explosion in the number of things that you could represent, and you don't necessarily have any way of steering yourself through that space toward the kinds of concepts that are probable or which make sense in your current situation.
So you can kind of think infinitely many things. Things might be very out of distribution. You're both immensely powerful but immensely overwhelmed by possibilities.

rubrics.text: The response explains that compositionality produces a combinatorial explosion in the space of possible representations.
The response explains that compositional representational capacity does not itself ensure guidance toward concepts that are plausible in the current context.

items.question: How do you think comparisons between neural and symbolic methods can confound different styles of problem solving?
items.object: Comparing neural and symbolic methods for inductive learning
items.answer: I like how you described it as the type signature. The inputs and outputs of the symbolic and neural ways of solving problems are often very different. If you try to solve something which is a pure transformer, with implicit outputs like we did in the transduction model, you're not constructing these intermediate hypotheses. When you have these symbolic compositional languages, like when you're doing program synthesis, the actual type of the thing that you're trying to learn is different. When we think about comparing neural and symbolic methods, they often confound these different factors. In this work, we were comparing neural and symbolic, but also partly comparing these two different styles of problem solving: one where you look at a problem and think hard about an explicit way of solving it, a way you could maybe verbalize in a symbolic language, either in code or in language; and contrasting that with a more intuitive, implicit, more transductive way of making predictions. It just so happened that it was convenient to map onto this neural-symbolic divide. You can imagine inductive methods that search for a vector that describes how to solve a problem. In fact, there were ARC teams that did this, and it actually kind of works, which is really cool. As Zen was saying, there's a grid of possibilities, and we're trying to do a very careful study of these different ways of solving inductive learning problems.

items.question: How do you understand the value of combining induction and transduction on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus?
items.object: Combining induction and transduction on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus
items.answer: Interestingly, this relates to some classic findings in cognitive science where we know that there are certain kinds of problems where, if you ask people to think carefully and verbalize a solution, they actually get worse. For instance, if you try to have people infer a rule with exceptions, or if you have people do more of a statistical learning task, like learning associations between different symbols, having them think a bit and explicitly verbalize a solution can degrade performance. We know empirically this is true. There's a really nice paper from Tom Griffith showing that. LLMs also have similar splits. I think we were rediscovering this within the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus. We were finding that there were some kinds of problems where, if you have the system think hard and churn through many thousands of different possibilities and test them systematically, that's actually worse than having the system just blurt out an answer. Because transduction and induction are systematically sweeping through possibilities versus just blurting out the answer, and because you can check the correctness of induction, you can think systematically for a while and, if you fail to find anything that seems like a good explanation to you, fall back on your intuition. So there's a very natural way of ensembling or combining these two methods.

items.question: Why do you think a functional, program-based solution is more likely to generalize than neural-network interpolation?
items.object: Functional program-based induction versus neural-network interpolation
items.answer: I think that the functional version is more regularized, like it's harder for it to overfit. It's not impossible, but it's pretty tough to overfit with these modern high-level programming languages. They're just designed to express general-purpose computations. Neural networks can do that, particularly, as you were saying, in the large-data limit. They tend to eventually learn representations that start to capture the kind of stuff you want. But that's not always true. Often they interpolate around their data points. So I think if you can come up with a clear, explicitly verbalizable description that actually works for the problem you're trying to solve, then that's likely to generalize a lot better than just going with an intuitive, vector-based interpolation.

items.question: Why do you find Python more practical than domain-specific languages for the AI problems you care about?
items.object: Python versus domain-specific languages as representations for AI
items.answer: In the first generation of AI there's a saying: you can't learn what you can't represent. To attack that, like Spelke earlier, if your computational language explodes, too bad. Maybe you could represent it, but it's not really learnable in any practical sense. In DreamCoder and in a lot of other languages that use domain-specific languages, often you're just not able to represent all the stuff you could do in Python. Now there's a simple fix: you can introduce an escape hatch, which is that you have some primitives that upgrade your DSL, your domain-specific language, to actually be Turing complete. Then in some formal sense, you do cover all the stuff that you can do in Python. But the curse of compositionality bites you. You couldn't learn it in any practical sense. In my opinion, having worked with these DSLs and with lambda calculus, Python is just a lot more practical for the kinds of problems that we really care about. This is true in ARC. I think it's true when we're building LM agents. I think it's true when we're having visual question-answering systems. There's an interesting convergent evolution between the design of software engineering languages, which has caused them to converge on something that's really great for a lot of problems we care about in AI. They're not perfect. In this transduction-induction paper, we do see that Python is not actually covering all the stuff that we care about, but it's miles better than lambda calculus.

items.question: Do you think AI systems should develop programs and hypotheses through an iterative refinement process?
items.object: Iterative refinement of programs and hypotheses in AI systems
items.answer: Yes. I think it's hard to provide an argument why that has to be true. But at least intuitively, it seems quite hard to write exactly the right program in one shot all the time. So there's some value in constructing a model, a hypothesis, or a program, depending on the context, and revising that with more information. That more information could be: it doesn't work in some particular use cases, or it doesn't support the evidence. Most of the hypothesis development that we do as humans is of this form, both as an individual and as science as a whole. Science as a whole collectively finds hypotheses, and then we revise them communally in conferences like this. So it seems natural to say that we should build systems that have this kind of refinement process. One of the hard things in trying to mechanize this is how do you guide or reinforce good refinement paths? How do you say, “Okay, this mode of reasoning or this mode of refinement or this path of refinement is the good path versus this other path, which is bad”? Right now, in modern machine learning, people are doing this mostly based on either reinforcement from human examples or, if you've got a well-defined objective function, you can backpropagate the signal from the correct solution through the reasoning paths. But that's not always the case. It's not always possible. One of the big open questions is how can we build systems that reason, where part of reasoning is refining hypotheses, when we don't have a well-defined, easy-to-compute objective function that we can evaluate at the end? I think if you can solve that, you can do pretty well.

items.question: What do you see as crucial to making iterative hypothesis refinement work?
items.object: Checking progress during iterative hypothesis refinement
items.answer: I just want to reinforce exactly what Zenna said right there, which is a lot of this really hinges on being able to check that you're heading in the right direction.

items.question: How do you think about the role of checking correctness in learning world models, programs, and reasoning systems?
items.object: Checking correctness when learning world models, programs, and reasoning systems
items.answer: We see this in our own work together, when we're trying to learn world models or programs for ARC tasks, because we have some data we're trying to fit and we can check our fit to the data. You also see this in things like o1, where, to the best of my knowledge, they're mostly training it on math problems, where you can check if you got the answer right. It's a big open puzzle, and I'm not sure I have great ideas on how to do this when you can't really check if you got it right. I'm not really sure how to do that, but it does seem very important.

items.question: How do you understand the philosophy behind wake-sleep learning?
items.object: Wake-sleep learning
items.answer: The philosophy there is tightly connected to what you see in a lot of machine learning, where you train a bottom-up model based on synthetic data produced by a top-down process. Often we're trying to solve some kind of inverse problem in AI. In vision, we're trying to look at an image and infer the three-dimensional structure. But the forward process of inferring the image from the three-dimensional structure is a lot simpler. That's a rendering function. So in wake-sleep, you're taking some forward process. You're imagining or dreaming possible ways you could run forward. Then you're learning how to go backward. For learning a function or a program, this means you're imagining programs. You're running them. Then you're saying retrospectively, “I just imagined this thing and I did this thing. So when I see this kind of behavior, I should infer this kind of program.” What wake-sleep brings to the table, on top of just training on synthetic data, is a back-and-forth between learning from your own synthetic data and learning how to make better synthetic data. It's not just this big batch mode thing of lots of dreams and then some learning from dreams. You actually wake up, go into the world, try to solve problems, and then adjust your distribution of synthetic data based on the problems that you're solving. This allows you to adjust to distribution shifts. You might think the world works a certain way. You have certain kinds of dreams, you learn from those dreams, but then you wake up and see the world is different. During the next sleep cycle, your dreams shift to better match the world. There's really a cooperation between the wake and sleep cycles, interleaved inside this big batch of synthetic data.

items.question: Why do you think compositional programs are valuable for wake-sleep learning?
items.object: Compositional programs in wake-sleep learning
items.answer: I also think there's an abstract component here in intelligence systems, certainly in all AI models. There's this iterative expansion and compression, expansion and compression. We see it even in neural networks: you want to be able to cover a little bit more of the distribution. I think this is where compositionality comes in and why it's good to do wake-sleep with programs. When you have a compositional language, you can take an atomic piece of knowledge you learned earlier and glue it together in a way that you never actually saw, but is kind of plausible. What you might see, and you should equip your neural network to be prepared for that composition. I don't think this is really a thing you want to guard against. You don't want to say, “I need to tightly fit my dreams to match my waking experience.” You actually want them to go a little bit beyond that.

items.question: How do you see the relationship between DreamCoder’s explicit library learning and using large foundation models to generate code from past examples?
items.object: Explicit library learning and its approximation with large foundation models
items.answer: We're moving more and more toward ways of implicitly doing the kinds of things DreamCoder was doing, but building them on top of large foundation models. Instead of having an explicit library of symbolic concepts that the system is learning over time, it has code that it knows was good in the past, and it uses a neural network to produce similar code. This is effectively what library learning was doing. It was always saying, “I've written some code in the past. I'm going to learn some functions, and that will allow me to write similar code in the future.” Except now it's done in a softer, more probabilistic way. I think you want to do both. There's something really valuable about how software engineers write reusable libraries. But it's tough to write the correct library right now with AI systems. It's tough to automatically debug not just a program with AI, but a full library of programs. As a halfway measure, you can use in-context learning to approximate the kind of abstraction learning you would get from a library. But in the end, I think they are complementary. We're not ditching libraries. We're just saying there's a middle ground that's easy to implement and works reasonably well.

items.question: How would you test whether abstractions learned through program synthesis capture real-world causal relationships?
items.object: Testing whether learned abstractions capture real-world causal mechanisms
items.answer: I'd say you need to actually go out into the world. You need to have an agent that's in environments, and it needs to be testing that its model faithfully describes real causal mechanisms. It needs to have an action space to be able to do interventions and so on. When we're just trying to learn functions, it's kind of hard to tell that your abstractions are the right ones. There might be lots of equivalent ways of describing the same function space. But as soon as you put your agents in a world where they have to achieve a range of goals, or plan and intervene on things, then you can falsify these hypotheses. In program synthesis, you don't falsify a library. You just say this is not very useful right now. Maybe it'll be useful later, but it's not very useful. In contrast, if your program is making hard claims about how the world works, that's where you can say this is not faithful to the true causal mechanisms.

items.question: How do you think reward signals help determine which abstractions of an environment are valuable?
items.object: Reward signals as a constraint on learning useful abstractions
items.answer: One thing that's interesting about how people think about problems at different levels of abstraction is that the abstractions are often defined on the fly for each problem. There's not one ground-truth abstraction. The world gives you data, and you could do the kind of Sora or Genie-type world model where you truly model the full data and capture all the pixels, or you could do the kind of thing that we're advocating for where you deliberately discard information. When you do that, I think the problem just becomes underconstrained. In order to introduce those extra constraints needed to tell you what abstractions are valuable, the easiest thing—and something that certainly works—is to introduce reward. If you give a reward signal in the environment, then you can say that a good tower of abstractions, even if it's on multiple levels, is one which allows you to plan to achieve reward. You see this in MuZero, where they're learning an abstract world model that isn't fully generative. It just predicts reward, policy, value, and so on. In some work we've done recently, we had simulated robot environments where robots interact with environments to use a tool or a mechanism. It sees pixels, but then it tries to define some abstractions on top of that, and the abstractions deliberately ignore a bunch of details. This was work led by Yichao Liang. It's called VisualPredicator. It was taking this MuZero perspective that someone gives you a reward signal.

items.question: How do you think people’s ability to form abstract models without being told a reward should inform program synthesis research?
items.object: Learning abstract models without an explicit reward signal
items.answer: What I think is really interesting is that even if you don't tell someone what the reward is, someone can still play with a new object or a new web app or a new appliance and form an abstract model. We're still thinking about exactly how that would work in a program synthesis context. A lot of the collaborations that we're planning right now are trying to answer that question, but I think it's very open. If you don't have reward, clearly humans can still figure out abstract models that, as Zenna was saying, omit a bunch of details, but it's trickier. It might connect to certain normative theories of intrinsic motivation. Or it might be something like wanting to be robust to a wide range of possible reward functions. There's a bunch of possibilities here.

items.question: How do you understand abstraction across programming languages and causal models?
items.object: Abstraction in programming languages and causal models
items.answer: It means different things in my context, for sure. But there's always an element of hiding details. In programming languages, a factor is often synonymous with a lambda expression. It's a function. It has variables and it's ignoring what values those variables take on. That is a sense in which a lambda abstraction is an abstraction. In what's sometimes called causal abstraction and causality, there's also an analogy or relation between two different causal models. The more abstract one is the one that's ignoring details, but still preserving some kind of essence of what the underlying causal model is. It's a word that means different things in different situations. The analogy between all of them is that there's some hiding of details, but some retention of the essence.

items.question: How do you think richer representations could improve approaches to solving ARC grid-transformation problems?
items.object: Abstract program representations for solving ARC grid-transformation problems
items.answer: One thing that's true at the moment about the primitives that we put in is that they correspond directly to transformations to the ARC grid. Conceptually, I think it would be cool to add these galaxy-brain principles. But what do they correspond to in terms of the actual transformation that we're trying to construct? One promising area for newer ARC approaches is precisely abstraction in the model, the program, the transformation program itself. What I mean is that right now our approach and many others synthesize something like a Python program, or literally a Python program, and then we apply this Python program to the input to get the output. But that Python program is fully formed. It's not abstract. It has all of its details there. You can run it, and that's great because you can see if it works. Intuitively, when you solve an ARC problem—at least for myself, I can't speak for other people—you first find some abstract part of the rule. You're like, “Well, I know that this object translates into this other object, but I'm not quite sure what the actual color transformation is.” Then I can go from there and say, “Okay, what could be the actual color transformation?” Conceptually, you can think of it almost like you write a sketch of a program in your mind with some holes. This gives you a direction to try and fill in these holes. You might fill them in one way, evaluate, and then go back and say that's not quite right. We don't quite have methods that produce these abstract program representations. I think that's something we could actually build: a representation of ARC transformations which doesn't have all its details filled in, but is still useful as a partial solution on the way to a full solution. I think there's a lot of potential approaches of that form where we've enriched the knowledge representation. This isn't quite about building new ontological ideas. It's saying we can abstract our current representations, and that could be powerful.

items.question: How do you understand your own thought process when solving ARC puzzles?
items.object: Kevin Ellis’s conscious strategy for solving ARC puzzles
items.answer: Sometimes it's very intuitive and I can't quite describe in words exactly what I'm doing. It might be something more like, “Well, I just kind of denoise the inputs and imagine what it should be in the parts that I can't really see.” Some things are definitely just perceptual and difficult to say precisely, except that you just kind of see it, kind of denoise it. Other times it is a very systematic thought process. I jumble up in my head different ways of seeing it. I see if it looks like it's on the right track. I have half-formed hypotheses. It's a much more perceptual and dynamic process than just the Greenblatt style of spamming out thousands of programs, which, to be clear, we do that also. I do think it's a little bit dangerous to introspect too heavily. It's a little misleading, but I think even if you look at the kinds of mistakes that people make, they don't exactly look like the kinds of mistakes that these AI systems make. That means that maybe there's something about the dynamics of how we're constructing the solutions that we're not really capturing with any of these approaches.

items.question: How do you imagine an iterative programming approach to solving ARC problems could work?
items.object: An iterative, REPL-style approach to solving ARC problems
items.answer: I could imagine iteratively applying the induction model and the transduction model in sequence, all parts of it assuring that the types match. I can also imagine a REPL-style approach to trying to solve ARC. Suppose that you are given an ARC problem, and you had a REPL, an interpreter environment. Then you could write code, evaluate it, check, write more code. Instead of creating one big transformation that you run, you do it in a more step-by-step process where you're continuously analyzing your current solution, writing some more code, checking it. I imagine there are approaches to ARC—and we're pursuing some of these—which look a little bit more like that: a step-by-step process where each step is producing code, and that code could be normal Python code or a transduction-like transformation, ultimately to get to a solution.

items.question: Why do you think iterative refinement and compositional knowledge matter for an agent learning to interact with the world?
items.object: Iterative refinement and compositional knowledge in agents
items.answer: I strongly agree with refining a solution over time. In some sense, you don't need it so much in ARC because you're solving just one problem at a time. But if you think about an agent in a world that's learning how to interact with many different causal mechanisms, then your agent needs to accumulate knowledge over time. It needs to revise its beliefs. If you had something which was more factored, like a DAG, or anything that breaks up the knowledge even more compositionally, so it's not just one program, it's lots of little programs that are all cooperating, then I think it would also be better at ARC, and closer to what you need for something that can grow its knowledge over time.

items.question: How do you judge whether an approach to solving François Chollet's ARC benchmark captures its intended spirit?
items.object: Approaches to solving François Chollet's ARC benchmark
items.answer: Surely he's said several times that ARC is an imperfect benchmark. I think there are ways to try and solve ARC which don't necessarily lead to the fundamental insight that you might want or that Chollet might want, and there are ways which are more fundamental. I think the approach that we've taken is a mixture of both. We've certainly got some ARC hacks in there to try and make it work. There are also certainly some fundamental ideas in there that we're trying to pursue. In terms of this expanding horizon, the more that you're trying to specialize to the particularities of ARC and build a DSL by going through and saying, “Okay, this is a useful element of ARC problems; this includes that; this is another useful element,” the more you're diverging a little bit from the essence of the intention of ARC. But there's an open question of how much of that is necessary. You need inductive biases to solve ARC; they have to come from somewhere. I asked François Chollet this several months ago: do you think a tabula rasa approach could solve ARC just from the examples within ARC? Is there enough information in the ARC dataset as a whole? He thinks there is. He thinks that if you condition on all of the ARC problems, then that's sufficient to solve ARC; you don't need to pre-train on internet data. But it's empirically true that the best solutions are at least partially pre-trained on internet data. I think the ideal solution to ARC would be simple and elegant and wouldn't require lots of ARC-related hacks and tricks. A robust way to try and get there is to introduce other problems which are related or in the spirit of ARC, or capture some of the same things but are not quite ARC, and force solutions which work on ARC and these other problems to push against ARC-specific domain hacks that humans might encode.

items.question: How do you see MARA, your project with Zenna, as a way to improve on ARC?
items.object: MARA's interactive approach to learning from few examples
items.answer: We want to have something which is in a lot of ways in the spirit of ARC. We're trying to learn something from very few examples and then generalize to new situations, but where you get to interact with something. So it's not quite an MDP, it's not like reinforcement learning, it's more like a model-building exercise. I think that this makes it a lot harder in some ways to just generate synthetic problems, which we did, because it's a little trickier to generate lots of synthetic interactive environments. You could do it, and I'm sure that we will try to do it. But it's at least one way of introducing a forcing function that causes you not to overfit so much.

items.question: How do you explain the empirical differences between transduction and induction on ARC reasoning problems?
items.object: The empirical differences between transduction and induction on ARC problems
items.answer: A lot of it just comes down to representations of models or transformations. Programming languages are a good way to think about it. A neural network is a program in a class of programs, the class of neural network programs, and a Python program is obviously a program. For any particular representation, there are some things that are going to be easier to encode and some things that are going to be harder to encode. If the languages are universal, then everything is possible, but some things are easier and some things are harder. It turns out that at least in some class of ARC problems, some are easier to encode as Python programs and some are easier to encode as direct neural transformations. Again, I think it's important to separate two different distinctions within transduction and induction. One is what I'm talking about now: the programmatic representation. The other is the type of the objects, the type signature of the object that you're constructing. Is your system producing a function which takes an ARC instance as input and outputs an ARC instance? Or is it a function that takes the entire ARC problem as input and directly produces the solution? I think we somewhat confounded those two things within the submission. You could separate those things and explore the different combinations, and I think that would lead to different trade-offs. To be more concrete, Python programs are good at expressing loops, deterministic computations, things where you've got maybe an unbounded or variable-bounded number of computations. The transformer model is a finite model. It has one pass and produces an output. There's a lot of interesting work showing that this corresponds to a particular class of computations. There are things you can express within that and things you can't. A lot of it comes down to the representation of programs.

items.question: How do you understand the different strengths of neural networks and Python programs for solving ARC problems?
items.object: Neural networks versus Python programs for solving ARC problems
items.answer: I don't really have a theoretical handle on that. I can't justify theoretically why a neural network should be able to do computations that are really tough to do in Python. It's an empirical fact. Obviously, Python can do things that a neural net is going to really struggle with. In the paper, we found things like counting or wanting to systematically do the same thing to every single object. Python is great for that. The other stuff is hard to really theoretically justify. I can just say it's empirical. It's definitely true. We ran the induction-transduction model with different random seeds. We wanted to make sure this was not just an artifact of randomness. It really is empirically the case that there are certain kinds of ARC problems, and I think many other kinds of problems, where Python in principle could do it, but a neural network is just much better for the job.

items.question: How do you see your program induction by example work with Wen-Ding as a way to bring DreamCoder-style wake-sleep learning into modern program synthesis?
items.object: Program induction by example using a language-model-based wake-sleep cycle
items.answer: That paper in some sense was our first attempt at trying to do something like wake-sleep in the DreamCoder style, but in a modern LM setting. It starts with some human-written programs, on the order of 10 to 100, and this defines implicitly a generative model over code, because you can prompt an LM with these example programs and then it will make up similar programs. So we have essentially a forward model. We can imagine programs. This gives us the dreaming phase of sleep because we can imagine these programs, run them, see what they do, and then train a program synthesizer based on these programs that we generate. We found that just doing this was pretty good at program synthesis problems. It was, frankly, a lot more effective than most of the lambda calculus stuff that I did in my PhD, and it substituted a lot of symbolic machinery with neural machinery. In doing so, it was able to take advantage of a lot of the advances in scale that we've had in recent years. What I've described so far—making synthetic data and then training a synthesizer on it—was what gave us the induction model for the ARC paper with Wen-Ding. We also introduced a full wake-sleep cycle, where it then tried to solve problems, remembers those solutions, and dreams about variations of those solutions. This means that if your prior is mismatched to what you really care about—for example, imagine you only think you need to write short programs, but the real world has long programs—then you can pre-train on short dream data, go out and encounter harder problems, solve a few of them, and during the next sleep cycle fine-tune your model to this new data distribution. It doesn't have the library-learning component of DreamCoder. It has a softer neural in-context-learning type of generative model. We're trying to bring this wake-sleep cycle into program synthesis in a more modern, more scalable setting.

items.question: What do you find exciting about Project MARA's approach to learning through interaction?
items.object: Project MARA's approach to learning through interaction
items.answer: This is very ARC-like in the sense that you're building a model on the fly from very small amounts of data. But you are not passively receiving the data. You have to go out there and poke things and push things and try things out. Zenna and I both did grad school in the cognitive science departments, and I think as a cognitive scientist—well, cognitive-science-adjacent—it's very exciting from that perspective. This is the kind of thing that is science-like, that humans do in everyday life. But I think it's also practically important because increasingly we're building these AI agents in both digital and physical worlds. They work well as long as their prior is well-aligned with the kind of environment they're already in. But when they're faced with a new kind of web page, or if you imagine a robot that has to figure out how to use a new kind of dishwasher and has to experiment with different buttons, that's quite hard. The more abstract kind of knowledge you need to learn—that, I think, is a really exciting challenge.
